title: Top-coordinate convolution pairing for truncated polynomial bialgebras
statement:
Let $F$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field], let $r\geq1$, $q=p^r$, and $n\geq0$. Let
$$C=F[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/(t_1^q,\ldots,t_n^q),$$
where the polynomial algebra is the commutative $F$-algebra freely generated by the displayed variables and the quotient imposes the displayed relations. Give $C$ unital $F$-algebra maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_F C$ and $\varepsilon:C\to F$ with $\varepsilon(t_i)=0$, satisfying $(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta$ and $(\varepsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta=\operatorname{id}_C$, under the tensor associativity and unit identifications [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The tensor algebra has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$. Put $H=\operatorname{Hom}_F(C,F)$, with convolution $(ab)(f)=(a\otimes b)(\Delta f)$ and unit $\varepsilon$ [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra]. Put $\omega=t_1^{q-1}\cdots t_n^{q-1}$ and $L(h)=h(\omega)$. Then the bilinear pairing
$$H\times H\longrightarrow F,\qquad (a,b)\longmapsto L(ab)$$
is nondegenerate in both arguments: $L(ab)=0$ for every $a\in H$ implies $b=0$, and $L(ab)=0$ for every $b\in H$ implies $a=0$. No cocommutativity of $\Delta$, antipode, grading compatibility, algebraic closedness or perfection of $F$ is assumed. For $n=0$ the conventions are $C=H=F$, $\omega=1$, and $L=\operatorname{id}_F$.

source.place: Agent algebra lemma for the finite-coordinate version of the distribution convolution construction of Chapter 10. No exact theorem of Milne is asserted to state this pairing. The elementary highest-total-degree proof is recorded in report.md; Jantzen I.8-I.9 is WANTED, not read.

proof.text: Put $A=\{\alpha\in\mathbf N^n:0\leq\alpha_i<q\}$, $\nu=(q-1,\ldots,q-1)$, $N=|\nu|=n(q-1)$ and $e_\alpha=t^\alpha$. Apply [lem-sfb-simultaneous-root-algebra-api] with coefficient ring $F$, tuple identically zero, number of variables $n$, and root exponent $q>0$. Its quotient is exactly $C$ and its displayed bounded monomials are an $F$-basis. Thus each $f\in C$ has a unique expansion $f=\sum_{\alpha\in A}f_\alpha e_\alpha$. Define $u_\alpha\in H$ by $u_\alpha(f)=f_\alpha$. These maps are linear, and any $h\in H$ is determined by the finitely many values $h(e_\alpha)$.

source.place: Agent proof, basis step; existing simultaneous-root power-basis lemma (Stacks 04GG, algebra.tex, lemma-characterize-henselian, proof of (10) implies (1)).

proof.text: By the tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], the elements $e_\alpha\otimes e_\beta$ span $C\otimes_F C$: expand both factors of each pure tensor in the preceding basis. They are independent, since the bilinear map $(f,g)\mapsto u_\gamma(f)u_\delta(g)$ induces a linear coefficient map which takes $e_\alpha\otimes e_\beta$ to $\delta_{\gamma\alpha}\delta_{\delta\beta}$. Write $x_i=t_i\otimes1$, $y_i=1\otimes t_i$, so these basis elements are $x^\alpha y^\beta$. Products add exponents, and are zero if an exponent reaches $q$; a nonzero product therefore preserves total degree. In particular the quotient relations never turn a high-degree monomial into one of smaller degree.

source.place: Agent proof, explicit tensor coordinates; Stacks 00CX, algebra.tex, lemma-tensor-product.

proof.text: Since $\varepsilon$ is an algebra map killing the $t_i$, it takes $e_0=1$ to $1$ and all other $e_\alpha$ to zero. Expand $\Delta(t_i)$ in the tensor basis. Applying $1\otimes\varepsilon$ fixes precisely its terms with second exponent zero, and the counit identity says their sum is $x_i$; applying $\varepsilon\otimes1$ similarly gives $y_i$. Therefore $\Delta(t_i)=x_i+y_i+R_i$, where every monomial of $R_i$ has both exponent vectors nonzero and hence total degree at least two. This conclusion uses both counit identities, without any symmetry assumption.

source.place: Agent proof, counit coefficient calculation in the basis of steps 1–2; Milne §9(d), p.174, counit convention.

proof.text: For $0\leq j<q$, let $c_j=\binom{q-1}{j}\cdot1_F$. In $F[Z]$, Frobenius iterated $r$ times gives $(1+Z)^q=1+Z^q$ [def-weil-ring-frobenius], since $F[Z]$ is commutative and $p\cdot1=0$. The binomial expansion [lem-sfb-commuting-binomial-expansion] gives $(1+Z)^{q-1}=\sum_{j<q}c_j Z^j$. Multiply by $1+Z$ and compare coefficients in degrees $0,\ldots,q-1$: $c_0=1$ and $c_j+c_{j-1}=0$ for $1\leq j<q$. Induction gives $c_j=(-1)^j$, which is nonzero, including in characteristic two.

source.place: Agent prime-power extension of the coefficient calculation in Milne Proposition 10.38 proof, printed p.205; Frobenius in Stacks 0CC6, varieties.tex, section-frobenius, paragraph after definition-absolute-frobenius (03SM).

proof.text:
Multiplicativity gives $\Delta(\omega)=\prod_i(x_i+y_i+R_i)^{q-1}$. In its distributive expansion there are $N$ factors; choosing only $x_i,y_i$ gives total degree $N$, while choosing any monomial of an $R_i$ gives degree at least $N+1$. By step 2 such a term either retains that degree or vanishes. Thus all coefficients of total degree below $N$ are zero, and its total-degree-$N$ part is $\prod_i(x_i+y_i)^{q-1}$. Using [lem-sfb-commuting-binomial-expansion] in the commutative tensor algebra, the coefficient $D_{\alpha, eta}$ of $e_\alpha\otimes e_ eta$ therefore satisfies
$$D_{\alpha, eta}=0\quad(|\alpha|+| eta|<N),\qquad D_{\alpha, eta}= egin{cases}\prod_i c_{\alpha_i}=(-1)^{|\alpha|}&\alpha+ eta=
u,\0&\alpha+ eta
e
u\end{cases}\quad(|\alpha|+| eta|=N).$$
There is no assertion about coefficients of larger total degree.

source.place: Agent proof, direct distributive and binomial expansion of the top monomial; Milne §9(d), p.174 and Proposition 10.38 proof, p.205 supply only conventions and the binomial calculation.

proof.text:
Let $b\in H$ be nonzero. Choose $ eta$ with $b(e_ eta)
e0$ of maximal total degree $d$ among its support, and put $\alpha=
u- eta$, a bounded exponent vector of degree $N-d$. By the convolution formula [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra],
$$L(u_\alpha b)=\sum_{\gamma\in A}D_{\alpha,\gamma}b(e_\gamma).$$
Terms with $|\gamma|<d$ vanish by the strict-degree inequality in step 5, terms with $|\gamma|>d$ vanish by choice of $d$, and among degree-$d$ terms only $\gamma= eta$ survives. Hence $L(u_\alpha b)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}b(e_ eta)
e0$. For nonzero $a\in H$, choose a maximal-degree support vector $\alpha$ for $a$ and set $ eta=
u-\alpha$. The same three cases, now summing the first exponent, give $L(a u_ eta)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}a(e_\alpha)
e0$. These are the contrapositives of the two asserted implications. For $n=0$, $A$ contains just the empty vector, $N=0$, and both calculations are ordinary multiplication in $F$ with $\omega=1$ and $L=\mathrm{id}_F$.
